summary: Describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax, used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt messages. It was replaced by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS is a common envelope for protected data. It defines the structures for a signed message, an encrypted message, a digest, and a message authentication code, so that different applications can protect their data in a way that other implementations can read.

questions: what is the difference between enveloped data and signed data
how does cms encrypt for multiple recipients
subtitle: A syntax for putting digital signatures, digests, encryption and message authentication codes into one envelope.

tldr.problem: Applications that need to sign, encrypt, digest or authenticate data needed one agreed envelope format, and the older PKCS #7 format could not carry everything they needed.
tldr.mechanism: CMS defines a ContentInfo object that carries a content type identifier and the content itself, and defines six content types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data. The values are ASN.1 structures encoded with BER, so they can be nested and processed in one pass.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2630 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370.

facts.label: Padding rule
facts.value: k-(lth mod k) octets, each with that value

sections.title: What CMS Is
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax describes an encapsulation syntax for data protection. It supports digital signatures, message authentication codes and encryption. The syntax allows multiple encapsulation, so one envelope can be nested inside another, and one party can digitally sign previously encapsulated data. It also allows arbitrary attributes, such as a signing time, to be signed along with the message content, and provides for other attributes such as countersignatures to be associated with a signature.

CMS is derived from PKCS #7 version 1.5 as specified in RFC 2315. Wherever possible, backward compatibility is preserved, but changes were necessary to accommodate attribute certificate transfer and key agreement techniques for key management. The syntax can support a variety of architectures for certificate-based key management, such as the one defined by the PKIX working group.

CMS values are generated using ASN.1 with BER encoding, and values are typically represented as octet strings. While many systems can transmit arbitrary octet strings reliably, many electronic mail systems cannot; this document does not address mechanisms for encoding octet strings for reliable transmission in such environments, and that job belongs to the mail layer.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is a container format for protected data. It started as a revision of PKCS #7 and adds what applications needed: certificates of other kinds, key agreement, and nesting so that a message can be encrypted and then signed.

sections.title: The ContentInfo Envelope
sections.content:
CMS is general enough to support many different content types. This document defines one protection content, ContentInfo, which encapsulates a single identified content type, and that identified type may provide further encapsulation. Six content types are defined: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data. Additional content types can be defined outside the document, and when they are, the ASN.1 type defined should not be a CHOICE type.

An implementation that conforms to this specification must implement the protection content ContentInfo, and must implement the data, signed-data and enveloped-data content types. The other content types may be implemented if desired.

The general syntax associates a content type identifier with a content. The syntax has the ASN.1 type ContentInfo, which holds a contentType field and a content field. The contentType is an object identifier, a unique string of integers assigned by an authority that defines the content type, and the type of the content can be determined uniquely from it. The content itself is the associated content.

As a general design philosophy, each content type permits single pass processing using indefinite-length BER encoding. Single-pass operation is especially helpful if the content is large, stored on tape, or piped from another process. The significant drawback is that it is difficult to perform encode operations using DER in a single pass, since the lengths of the various components may not be known in advance. Signed attributes within the signed-data content type and authenticated attributes within the authenticated-data content type do require DER encoding, and they must be transmitted in that form so that recipients can verify content that contains one or more unrecognized attributes. Signed attributes and authenticated attributes are the only CMS data types that require DER encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CMS object has the same outer shape: a label saying what kind of content it holds, and the content itself. The label is a number registered by an authority. Because the encoding allows an indefinite length, a large object can be processed as it streams past.

sections.title: Signing Data
sections.content:
The signed-data content type consists of a content of any type and zero or more signature values, and any number of signers in parallel can sign any type of content. The typical application represents one signer's digital signature over content of the data type; another typical application disseminates certificates and certificate revocation lists.

The construction takes four steps. For each signer, a message digest is computed on the content with a signer-specific digest algorithm; if the signer is signing information other than the content, the digest of the content and that other information are digested together and the result becomes the message digest. The message digest is then digitally signed with the signer's private key. The signature value and other signer-specific information are collected into a SignerInfo value, together with the signer's certificates and revocation lists and any others not corresponding to a signer. Finally, the digest algorithms and the SignerInfo values of all the signers are collected together with the content into a SignedData value.

A recipient independently computes the message digest and uses it with the signer's public key to verify the signature. The public key is referenced either by an issuer distinguished name along with an issuer-specific serial number, or by a subject key identifier that uniquely identifies the certificate holding the key, and the signer's certificate may be included in the SignedData certificates field.

The signed content is carried in an EncapsulatedContentInfo structure, which holds a content type identifier and the content itself as an octet string; the content need not be DER encoded. Omitting the content field makes it possible to construct external signatures, where the content being signed is absent from the signed-data value and the signature value is calculated as though it were present.

Each SignerInfo holds the signer's identifier, the digest algorithm, the signed attributes, the signature algorithm, the signature itself, and optional unsigned attributes. The signed attributes must be present when the content type being signed is not id-data, and if present they must contain at least a content-type attribute holding the content type of the signed content and a message-digest attribute holding the digest of the content.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign, the sender hashes the content, signs the hash with the private key, and puts the signature, the hash algorithm and any signed details such as the signing time into the envelope. The receiver hashes the content again and checks the signature against it.

sections.title: Encrypting Data for Recipients
sections.content:
The enveloped-data content type consists of an encrypted content of any type and encrypted content-encryption keys for one or more recipients. The combination of the encrypted content and one encrypted content-encryption key for a recipient is a digital envelope for that recipient, and any type of content can be enveloped for an arbitrary number of recipients using any of the three key management techniques for each recipient.

The construction takes five steps. A content-encryption key is generated at random for the chosen content-encryption algorithm. That key is then encrypted for each recipient, and three general techniques are supported: key transport, where the content-encryption key is encrypted in the recipient's public key; key agreement, where the recipient's public key and the sender's private key generate a pairwise symmetric key and the content-encryption key is encrypted in that key; and symmetric key-encryption keys, where the content-encryption key is encrypted in a previously distributed symmetric key. The encrypted key and other recipient-specific information go into a RecipientInfo value. The content is then encrypted with the content-encryption key, and the RecipientInfo values for all recipients are collected with the encrypted content to form an EnvelopedData value.

A recipient opens the digital envelope by decrypting one of the encrypted content-encryption keys and then decrypting the content with the recovered key. Each key management technique has its own RecipientInfo type: KeyTransRecipientInfo for key transport, KeyAgreeRecipientInfo for key agreement, and KEKRecipientInfo for previously distributed symmetric keys, whose version is always 4.

For content encryption, the data is padded at the trailing end so that its length is a multiple of the block size k: the input is padded with k minus the input length modulo k octets, all having that value. The padding can be removed unambiguously because all input is padded, including values that are already a multiple of the block size, and no padding string is a suffix of another. This padding method is well defined if and only if k is less than 256.
sections.plainLanguage: To encrypt, the sender makes a random key for the content, encrypts the content with it, and encrypts that key separately for each recipient. The recipient unwraps its copy of the key and decrypts the content. Only the key travels to each recipient in a form only it can open.

sections.title: Digesting, Encrypting and Authenticating Data
sections.content:
The digested-data content type consists of content of any type and a message digest of the content. It is typically used to provide content integrity, and the result generally becomes an input to the enveloped-data content type. A message digest is computed on the content with a message-digest algorithm, and the algorithm and the digest are collected together with the content into a DigestedData value. A recipient verifies the digest by comparing it with an independently computed digest.

The encrypted-data content type consists of an encrypted content of any type, and the content is encrypted with a content-encryption key in the same way as the enveloped-data type, but without the recipient information that carries the key to the recipients.

The authenticated-data content type consists of content of any type, a message authentication code, and encrypted authentication keys for one or more recipients. The combination of the MAC and one encrypted authentication key for a recipient is necessary for that recipient to verify the integrity of the content, and any type of content can be integrity protected for an arbitrary number of recipients. A message-authentication key is generated at random, encrypted for each recipient, and the originator computes a MAC value on the content with that key. If the originator is authenticating information in addition to the content, a message digest is calculated on the content, and the digest and the other information are authenticated with the key to produce the MAC value.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides signing and encrypting, CMS can carry a plain digest of some content, content encrypted with a key that is not distributed inside the message, and a message authentication code, which lets a holder of a shared key check that the content was not changed.

sections.title: Algorithms, Key Protection and Known Attacks
sections.content:
Section 12 lists the algorithms this document supports: SHA-1 and MD5 for digests, DSA and RSA for signatures, key agreement with X9.42 ephemeral-static Diffie-Hellman and key transport with RSA for key management, Triple-DES and RC2 key wrap for symmetric key-encryption keys, Triple-DES CBC and RC2 CBC for content encryption, and HMAC with SHA-1 for message authentication codes.

The security considerations state that implementations must protect the signer's private key, since compromising it permits masquerade, and must protect the key management private key, the key-encryption key and the content-encryption key. Compromise of the key management private key or the key-encryption key may disclose all messages protected with that key, and compromise of the content-encryption key may disclose the associated encrypted content.

Implementations must randomly generate content-encryption keys, message-authentication keys, initialization vectors and padding. Inadequate pseudo-random number generators can result in little or no security, because an attacker may find it much easier to reproduce the generator environment than to brute force the whole key space. The RFC points at RFC 1750 for guidance on generating quality random numbers.

When the key-encryption and content-encryption algorithms differ, the effective security is determined by the weaker of the two. If content is encrypted with 168-bit Triple-DES and the Triple-DES content-encryption key is wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key, then at most 40 bits of protection is provided, so implementers must ensure that key-encryption algorithms are as strong or stronger than content-encryption algorithms. Implementers should also be aware that cryptographic algorithms become weaker with time, and should keep implementations modular so that new algorithms can be inserted as the set of mandatory algorithms changes.

Finally, users of CMS should be aware that PKCS #1 Version 1.5 as specified in RFC 2313 is vulnerable to adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks when applied for encryption. The attack needs an oracle that responds to a large number of ciphertexts, so it appears less feasible for store-and-forward S/MIME than for interactive protocols, but it is more feasible where CMS is an intermediate encryption layer in an interactive exchange. PKCS #1 Version 2.0 resolves the problem by recommending Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding when RSA is used for confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: The weak link decides the security: if a content key is protected by a weaker algorithm, the whole message is only as strong as that weaker algorithm. Keys must be generated randomly and kept secret, and the RSA padding of PKCS #1 Version 1.5 has a known weakness in interactive use.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO DELIVER A CONTENT KEY

items.title: Key transport
items.text: The content key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.

items.title: Key agreement
items.text: The recipient's public key and the sender's private key make a pairwise key that wraps the content key.

items.title: Symmetric key wrapping
items.text: The content key is encrypted in a key that was distributed to both sides earlier.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH KIND OF CMS CONTENT GIVES YOU

cells: Content plus one or more signatures
Proof of who signed and that the content was not changed
Encrypted content plus an encrypted key per recipient
The content, once it opens its own copy of the key
Content plus a message authentication code
Proof of integrity for anyone holding the shared key
Encrypted content, with no key inside
The content, if it already holds the key
